title: I built an open-source tool that lets you walk through a codebase as a 3D city
summary:
Understanding an unfamiliar codebase can be frustrating. You jump between files, documentation, and architecture diagrams trying to figure out how everything connects.

I wanted to experiment with a different approach.

So I built Kodyurd, an open-source tool that turns local codebases into explorable 3D cities.


You can walk through modules, explore architecture diagrams, replay source-backed flows, and learn how the system works through interactive lessons.

It runs locally and uses your existing Claude Code or Codex setup for generation.

The project is MIT-licensed and still in early development.

GitHub: https://github.com/azerturk/kodyurd

I'm particularly interested in feedback from developers who regularly explore unfamiliar repositories.

title: Auditable AI billing without a blockchain: signed batches and their limits
summary:
The difficult part of AI API billing is often the request that almost finished. The router sent the prompt, the provider began responding, and the connection disappeared before final usage arrived. A database can store a precise number for that request without making the number well justified.

I am building TeeRouter, and this led to two separate design questions: what evidence supports a charge, and how can someone later detect changes to the published accounting records?

The implementation borrows a useful idea associated with blockchains: publish cryptographically verifiable records that readers can inspect independently. It does not run a blockchain or claim decentralized consensus. This article examines the public source at commit 5c89b551; it is an implementation case study, not an independent certification of the deployed service.

First define what a charge means

A receipt should preserve the pricing decision used for that request. Looking up today's price when displaying last week's usage makes historical charges difficult to reproduce.

TeeRouter freezes the pricing revision, applicable rules, and pool multiplier at admission. Provider-specific calculators interpret native usage fields. The basis is public API list pricing multiplied by the pool's multiplier, not a claim about the merchant's actual subscription expenditure or negotiated invoice.

The billing implementation uses integer arithmetic, retains pre-rounding amounts, and rounds upward once per request to micro-USD. This makes the chosen calculation reproducible without promising to match a provider's monthly invoice rounding, taxes, or discounts.

For a simple illustrative quote, 10,000 ordinary input tokens at $2 per million plus 1,000 output tokens at $8 per million produces a $0.028 base cost. A 1.2 multiplier gives $0.0336. These are made-up rates, not a current model quotation. Real records must also distinguish cached input, applicable pricing dimensions, and how each provider reports usage.

A timeout is an observation, not a usage counter

The interrupted-request policy separates several outcomes:

Observed outcome Accounting treatment
Router rejects the request before forwarding No charge
Upstream rejects it with HTTP 3xx/4xx No charge; any reported counters are retained as waived usage
Sending fails before the complete request is flushed, with no generation evidence No charge
Complete request is flushed, then the connection fails before a reply Estimate input at ordinary input pricing; no unseen output
Generation starts, then delivery fails Use official counters where available and estimates for supported missing portions
A successful response has missing or invalid usage Preserve an explicit pending reason

A generated refusal inside a successful model response is different from an HTTP rejection: generation may have consumed billable tokens.

The controversial row is the timeout after a full flush. A successful local flush does not prove that the remote application received or executed the request. The policy chooses a financial treatment for that ambiguity; it does not eliminate the ambiguity. Customers need to know that an estimated input charge can occur at this boundary.

Estimation is restricted to failed or interrupted model requests and is labelled estimated or mixed, with partial coverage. Unknown hidden output is not invented. A downstream cancellation cancels the upstream operation rather than draining it in the background, although closing a connection cannot guarantee the provider immediately stops computing.

Publishing these distinctions matters more than making every row appear confidently “settled.” A signed estimate remains an estimate.

Sign a batch, retain the exact bytes

The current public receipt format signs batches of records. A manifest includes the boot and key identity, batch number, previous hash, sequence range, record digest, count, and calculated total.

Conceptually, verification follows this chain:

original record bytes -> SHA-256 digest -> manifest
manifest + protocol label -> Ed25519 signature
manifest -> reference to preceding batch

There is one signature per batch. The current public format does not have per-record Merkle inclusion proofs. A reader needs the original complete records_json to verify the records; reserializing JSON may change the bytes being checked.

The verifier distinguishes a valid signature from an independently trusted TEE signing identity. The latter also requires hardware evidence and an approved reference policy. It is not established by a public key or a “verified” label included in the downloaded bundle.

Hash links let readers check continuity between supplied batches. They do not create consensus, prove that an operator has disclosed the latest batch, or prove that no other history exists. Independently retaining known batch heads could strengthen monitoring, but that is a separate system property, not something the signature supplies automatically.

Storage acknowledgment is not settlement

Consider a batch that reaches external storage, followed by a lost acknowledgment. Regenerating it with new metadata would complicate duplicate detection. TeeRouter freezes the signed bytes before upload and resends those same bytes on a later cycle.

A valid durable-storage acknowledgment permits releasing the uploaded raw details. It does not reset consumption or update user balances. Per-user, per-batch summaries remain until a separate settlement acknowledgment applies a balance update through an identified uploaded head.

That boundary is necessary because requests may finish while settlement is happening. Retiring consumption only through the acknowledged head preserves newer charges. Revisions and idempotent retries prevent repeating the same settlement from applying it twice.

The default upload cycle is five minutes. That is a delivery schedule, not a guarantee of completeness or immediate publication.

What survives a restart?

The optional accounting journal stores committed events and delivery state in SQLite WAL with authenticated encryption. Frozen batches keep their original signatures after restart; new batches use the new process identity.

It protects successfully committed records. It cannot reconstruct an in-flight request that never produced an event, recover usage that was never observed, or prevent deletion or rollback of an entire journal copy. On a journal write failure or capacity limit, the implementation closes new admission instead of silently discarding accepted events.

This makes durability a concrete, bounded claim rather than “nothing can ever be lost.”

Public accounting without publishing conversations

Public batches exclude prompts, answers, credentials, and refusal text. They contain accounting fields and refusal categories. User pseudonyms rotate using a fresh public batch nonce and a private random identity, rather than hashing a short username.

That reduces direct linkage across batches but does not guarantee anonymity. Timing, model choices, merchant identifiers, and distinctive traffic volumes can still correlate activity.

The resulting ledger is useful because readers can check the bytes they received, inspect charge evidence, and distinguish estimates from observed usage. Deposits, withdrawals, externally managed balances, missing history, and provider-side execution remain separate questions. Keeping those boundaries explicit is what makes the evidence meaningful.

title: What a TEE can actually prove about an AI API router
summary:
An AI API router sits in an awkward place. It needs to read a request to select an upstream account, enforce permissions, and calculate usage. That also gives its operator opportunities to change parameters, misuse credentials, or report a different price from the one the client expected.

Publishing the router's source helps people inspect those decisions. It leaves another question unanswered: is that the program handling my request?

I am building TeeRouter, an open-source router that explores this question using trusted execution environments and independently verifiable receipts. This is a case study of its public implementation at commit 5c89b551, rather than an independent audit or verification of a live deployment. The interesting part is how narrow the useful guarantees need to be.

Start with the connection

Suppose a service presents a valid hardware attestation report. If the report is unrelated to the TLS connection carrying your prompts, it tells you very little about where those prompts go. An untrusted frontend could show evidence from a legitimate enclave while processing requests somewhere else.

TeeRouter binds its current TLS certificate and a client-generated challenge into the attestation report. The binding in the channel implementation is:

REPORT_DATA = SHA512(
    UTF8("teellm:attested-channel:v1\0")
    || nonce32
    || SHA256(certDER)
)

The nonce gives the verifier a freshness challenge. The certificate digest connects the evidence to the certificate used for TLS. The protocol label separates this purpose from other uses of attestation data.

This only works if the client actually checks that binding and uses the corresponding authenticated connection. Downloading a report, displaying a green badge, and then sending traffic to an unrelated endpoint would discard the useful property.

A hardware signature is only the beginning

An authentic report can still describe a program you should not trust. A verifier needs an independently chosen policy defining which measurements and security state it accepts.

For the TDX path, the project checks certificate chains, revocation and trusted computing base information, measurements, the relevant event sequence, and the report-data binding. The security document makes the independence requirement explicit: evidence supplied by the server cannot also be the sole authority deciding what counts as trustworthy.

There is an operational consequence here. Updating the router is also a trust-policy problem. A client must have a defensible reason to accept the new measured software. Automatically trusting every measurement announced by the service would weaken the point of checking measurements at all.

The application also matters. A correctly attested program with a credential-export endpoint would still export credentials. TEE isolation does not repair bad authorization logic, unsafe dependencies, or mistakes in the approved code. It reduces particular infrastructure trust assumptions under its hardware and software threat model; it does not remove the need for review.

Separate the administrator from the person making a request

A router administrator needs to change balances and permissions. That does not mean the administrator should be able to impersonate a user and spend their balance.

The current user authentication protocol requires a client-owned Ed25519 signature as well as a valid Bearer credential. A user ID is derived from the public key; the signing seed stays with the client.

The signature covers the exact body bytes, method, path and query, relevant headers, a timestamp, a random nonce, and the router's boot ID. Including authorization and routing headers prevents someone from preserving the body while silently changing the account-pool selection or other signed instructions. Including a boot ID makes proofs from an earlier process invalid after a restart.

This is a deliberately limited separation of powers. An administrator can still deny service, change permission settings, or alter externally managed balances. What administrator authority alone cannot do, under the verified implementation, is produce a valid signature for the existing user's key.

Preserve the request, including the expensive details

AI requests carry more financially significant settings than a model name. Cache controls, service tiers, reasoning options, and tool definitions can all affect behavior or cost.

TeeRouter's documented forwarding boundary preserves native generation parameters instead of silently adding its own cache or retention choices. Account egress is explicitly configured, official upstream HTTPS certificates remain checked, and a failed proxy is not supposed to fall back to a direct connection. These are application properties to inspect in the approved version, not properties hardware provides automatically.

There is also a boundary the router cannot cross: the upstream provider still receives the prompt. Attesting an intermediary does not attest the provider's internal inference service, prove which model weights it ran, or establish how it retains requests. A router can preserve a requested parameter; it cannot turn that parameter into independently observed behavior inside another company's infrastructure.

Evidence needs more than one status flag

The project also signs consumption batches. Its standalone verifier distinguishes signature verification, record verification, and TEE verification.

That distinction is useful beyond this project. A mathematically valid signature says that a key signed particular bytes. Hardware evidence and an approved reference policy can establish more about that key's origin. Neither result alone establishes that every request appears in the supplied history or that the latest batch has been disclosed.

For someone assessing a deployment, I would want separate answers to these questions:

  • Which software and reference policy did I approve?
  • Is this evidence fresh and bound to the connection I am using?
  • Which operations remain possible for the administrator?
  • Which data and decisions still depend on the upstream provider?
  • Which failures can interrupt availability or leave accounting incomplete?

Those answers are more useful than a single “TEE verified” label. The practical value is being able to inspect a specific program, verify a connection to an accepted instance, and understand exactly which remaining promises still require trust.

title: I Kept Generated Video Templates Editable Without Letting Them Drift
summary:
I needed a generated video to remain editable after a customer changed a headline, swapped an image, or asked for a different CTA. The dependable approach is to preserve one validated VideoJSON document, expose only the fields people should touch, then render from that same document. That keeps a template flexible without letting timing, branding, or media assumptions silently drift.

The tempting shortcut is to render the first MP4, let someone request changes in a separate editor, and hope the next version resembles the first. That loses the source of truth immediately. Instead, I treat the template as a small contract: generated data is an input, VideoJSON is the saved working document, an editor is the controlled change surface, and a renderer is the final delivery step.

The boundary that stopped template drift

A video template should not make every property editable merely because the timeline can support it. In a product, I divide fields into three buckets before opening an editor:

Field type Example Who can change it? Why
Locked structure scene order, duration budget, required legal frame developer or template owner protects the promise the template was designed to make
Safe content product name, price, image URL, CTA, locale generator and approved user controls expected variation
Guarded creative control crop, music level, transition choice user with validation can improve a result but can also break readability

That table is deliberately boring. It is also the part that prevents an innocent copy edit from becoming a 19-second product video with a missing CTA. If a field has a visual or compliance consequence, name its owner and validation rule before it gets into the UI.

VideoFlow is useful here because its core compiles an authored flow into portable VideoJSON, and the same document can drive a live preview, browser export, or server render. That is the important architectural detail—not that JSON is fashionable, but that preview, edit, and output are no longer three loosely related representations.

Generate data, then validate a video document

I do not send an LLM or a catalog row straight to an MP4 renderer. It should first produce a narrow input object, then a template function maps that object into the known video shape. The template owner remains responsible for defaults and timing.

import VideoFlow from "@videoflow/core";

type ProductInput = {
  title: string;
  imageUrl: string;
  cta: string;
};

export async function makeDraft(input: ProductInput) {
  const $ = new VideoFlow({ name: input.title, width: 1080, height: 1080, fps: 30 });

  $.addImage({ fit: "cover" }, { source: input.imageUrl });
  $.addText({ text: input.title, fontSize: 7, fontWeight: 800 });
  $.wait("2.5s");
  $.addText({ text: input.cta, fontSize: 4, fontWeight: 700 });

  return $.compile(); // save this VideoJSON before any render
}

In production I would validate title, imageUrl, duration, allowed font sizes, and asset domains around that function. The point is that the generated values fill known slots; they do not invent scene order, arbitrary effects, or a renderer configuration. This is the same principle behind the review gate in my earlier VideoJSON pipeline guide: make a structured draft inspectable before an expensive or irreversible step.

Let customers edit the document, not the output

When a person needs more than a form can offer, give them a constrained editing surface on the saved document. VideoFlow’s React Video Editor takes VideoJSON, offers a multi-track timeline and live preview, and returns changes through callbacks. Persistence remains my job.

import { VideoEditor } from "@videoflow/react-video-editor";
import "@videoflow/react-video-editor/style.css";

export function CustomerVideo({ video, save }: { video: unknown; save: (next: unknown) => Promise<void> }) {
  return (
    <VideoEditor
      video={video}
      theme="night"
      onChange={(next) => save(next)}
      onSave={async (next) => save(next)}
      onUpload={async (file) => ({ url: await uploadAsset(file), type: file.type })}
    />
  );
}

The component is not a permission system. I still enforce the contract server-side when saving: reject a changed frame rate, missing required layer, disallowed media URL, or a timeline beyond the duration budget. A UI restriction is a usability aid; validation is the actual safety boundary.

My four checks before an export enters a queue

Here is the small receipt I would save beside every render request:

  1. Source identity: template version, input ID, and a hash or revision of the VideoJSON.
  2. Structural validity: required scenes and layers exist; duration, resolution, and FPS meet the template rule.
  3. Asset readiness: every media URL is reachable and allowed by policy.
  4. Delivery choice: browser export for a user-operated, privacy-sensitive small job; server rendering for queues, batches, and APIs.

VideoFlow’s browser renderer can create an MP4 Blob client-side and supports progress plus cancellation; its server renderer is intended for headless Node jobs and queue-style work. I would choose based on where the job belongs, not based on where the template was authored. The document can stay the same.

That separation also makes failures explainable. If preview looks right but server output is wrong, compare the saved VideoJSON revision and renderer configuration. If a customer change breaks a scene, inspect the rejected validation rule rather than trying to reverse-engineer an MP4.

A practical rollout sequence

Start with one template, one input schema, and one user role. Store the compiled VideoJSON after generation, render a DOM preview, and let a tester change only copy and media. Then add the guarded controls one at a time.

For an example of why I keep a clear source-to-output handoff, see the publishing contract I added to an automation pipeline. The domain is different, but the discipline is the same: a saved contract gives reviewers something concrete to approve and debuggers something concrete to compare.

TL;DR

Keep VideoJSON as the editable source of truth. Generate data into a controlled template, validate every saved revision, expose only intentional edit controls, and render the exact approved revision in the environment that fits the job.

That is enough to make generated video feel flexible to customers without turning every request into a fresh manual timeline. What fields would you lock first in a customer-editable video template?

Here is the small receipt I would save beside every render request:

  1. Source identity: template version, input ID, and a hash or revision of the VideoJSON.
  2. Structural validity: required scenes and layers exist; duration, resolution, and FPS meet the template rule.
  3. Asset readiness: every media URL is reachable and allowed by policy.
  4. Delivery choice: browser export for a user-operated, privacy-sensitive small job; server rendering for queues, batches, and APIs.

VideoFlow’s browser renderer can create an MP4 Blob client-side and supports progress plus cancellation; its server renderer is intended for headless Node jobs and queue-style work. I would choose based on where the job belongs, not based on where the template was authored. The document can stay the same.

That separation also makes failures explainable. If preview looks right but server output is wrong, compare the saved VideoJSON revision and renderer configuration. If a customer change breaks a scene, inspect the rejected validation rule rather than trying to reverse-engineer an MP4.

A practical rollout sequence

Start with one template, one input schema, and one user role. Store the compiled VideoJSON after generation, render a DOM preview, and let a tester change only copy and media. Then add the guarded controls one at a time.

For an example of why I keep a clear source-to-output handoff, see the publishing contract I added to an automation pipeline. The domain is different, but the discipline is the same: a saved contract gives reviewers something concrete to approve and debuggers something concrete to compare.

TL;DR

Keep VideoJSON as the editable source of truth. Generate data into a controlled template, validate every saved revision, expose only intentional edit controls, and render the exact approved revision in the environment that fits the job.

That is enough to make generated video feel flexible to customers without turning every request into a fresh manual timeline. What fields would you lock first in a customer-editable video template?

title: How to Turn Speech into Text on a Computer
summary:
Typing a long text by hand is slow. We can speak faster than we type, so it is handy when the computer turns your speech into text by itself. Below is how to turn speech into text on a computer, and which way is simpler.

Why you might need it

  • Quickly write an email, a note or a message without typing.

  • Capture a thought before it slips away.

  • Turn a voice note into text.

  • Write when your hands are busy or tired.

Way 1. The built-in Windows voice typing

Windows has voice typing built in: press Win + H in any text field and speak. It is free and needs no installation. The downsides: it needs the internet, the settings are scattered around the system, and you often have to fix punctuation by hand.

Way 2. Online services

There are websites where you can speak into the microphone or upload a recording and get text back. Handy for a one-off task, but keep in mind: your voice goes to someone else's server. For personal or work recordings that is not always a good idea.

Way 3. A simple program on your computer

If you want it simple, with no fuss over settings, a dedicated program fits well. VoiceNote is made for exactly that: press “Record” and speak — the app types your speech as text for you. You can copy or save the finished text. The interface is simple: one Record button, one Stop button.

More about the VoiceNote program

How to dictate for cleaner text

  • Speak evenly and not too fast.

  • Make short pauses between phrases.

  • Record in a quiet place, with no background noise.

  • Check the finished text and fix the punctuation.

FAQ

Do I need an expensive microphone?**No. A regular laptop or headset microphone is fine — the main thing is to speak clearly.

Which language does it work in?****Russian and other languages.

Will my speech go to someone else's server?**
VoiceNote runs on your own computer and does not send texts outside.

In short

  • Fast and free — the built-in Windows voice typing (Win + H).

  • A one-off, non-personal task — online is fine.

  • Simple and on your own computer — VoiceNote: press Record, speak, get text.

title: We Took a 105K-LOC Flutter App from Zero Tests to 2,583
summary:
The app had 105,000 lines of Dart spread across 757 files. Firebase Remote Config, Firestore, FFI calls into Rust for GPS processing, SharedPreferences for half the state management. Zero tests.

Not "low coverage." Zero. No test directory, no test runner config, no mocks. Seven months of production use on 30 devices, and the first flutter test invocation in the project's history was mine.

I wrote a preprint documenting how we got from that zero to 2,583 tests across 292 files. The paper and all companion data are open access on Zenodo: DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24260880.

This post covers the key findings. The paper has the full methodology.

The Problem Nobody Warns You About

Every Flutter testing tutorial starts with a counter app. Tap a button, verify the number. That is not the hard part.

The hard part is a LocationService that wraps Geolocator, which wraps a platform channel, which talks to a GPS chip that returns different accuracy values depending on whether you're indoors, moving, or on a Huawei device where PowerGenie has throttled location updates to once every 15 minutes. You can't mock what you can't define the boundary for.

We had 43 platform-dependent classes. Each one touched at least one of: Firebase, native GPS via FFI, SharedPreferences, or package_info_plus. The first month was spent not writing tests, but drawing mock boundaries.

What Worked

Coverage-exclusion policy. We excluded generated files (*.g.dart, *.freezed.dart) and pure platform-channel wrappers from coverage metrics. Not from testing, from metrics. The distinction matters: we still tested the wrappers, but a wrapper that delegates to MethodChannel('gps') and returns the raw result has exactly one interesting failure mode (the channel throws), and counting its lines toward coverage targets distorts where effort should go.

Mock-boundary pattern. Every platform dependency got a thin abstract interface. The real implementation lives in one file; the mock in another. No when().thenReturn() chains longer than three lines. If the mock setup is more complex than the code it replaces, the boundary is in the wrong place.

17 custom lint rules via kx_lints. We published these as an open-source package on pub.dev. Three of the rules exist solely because test files kept importing production Firebase instances. One rule (no_direct_firebase_access) caught 23 violations in its first week. The rules are the cheapest part of the whole system: write once, enforce forever.

Six Cases Where Tests Caught Production Bugs

The paper documents six specific instances where the test suite caught bugs that would have reached production. I'll describe two here.

Case 1: GPS despiking. Our Rust FFI module processes raw GPS coordinates and filters spikes (sudden jumps that occur when the device switches between GPS and network location). A test for the despike threshold caught a regression where a refactor changed the spike detection from 200m to 2000m. That's the difference between "filters the occasional multipath reflection" and "filters nothing." The test failed, the commit was reverted, and 30 field workers never saw jumps in their route history.

Case 2: SharedPreferences race. Two cubits wrote to the same SharedPreferences key on shift-end. The tests caught this because they ran both cubits in sequence and asserted on the final state. In production, the race would have silently dropped punch-out timestamps for about 8% of shifts (we measured the frequency in staging after the tests flagged it).

The Numbers

  • 2,583 tests across 292 test files
  • 43 platform-dependent classes with clean mock boundaries
  • 17 custom lint rules (13 org-wide via kx_lints, 4 project-specific)
  • 6 documented cases where tests caught real production bugs before deployment

The companion repository is at github.com/GhagSagar23/zero-to-tested. The lint rules are at kx_lints on pub.dev.

What I'd Do Differently

I wouldn't start with unit tests. I'd start with the lint rules. Three weeks of writing tests before the no_direct_firebase_access rule existed meant three weeks of finding violations by hand in PR review. The lint rules should have come first; they're the cheapest safety net and they make every subsequent test easier to write correctly.

I also wouldn't chase 100% line coverage. We settled at a policy that excludes generated code and pure wrappers, and that policy is documented and enforced by CI. The number on the badge matters less than whether the tests actually catch the bugs that matter to your users.

The full paper is free to read: doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24260880

If you've done something similar in a Flutter codebase (or any mobile codebase with heavy platform integration), I'd like to hear how you handled the mock-boundary problem. Drop a comment or find me on GitHub.

title: How to Build 121+ Client-Side File Extraction Tools in Vanilla JS & WebAssembly
summary:
Whenever users need to inspect an unfamiliar file—whether extracting text from a scanned PDF, dumping sheets from an Excel workbook, decoding a sensitive JWT token, parsing financial bank statements (MT940/BAI2), or inspecting headers inside a Windows PE/MSI installer—the standard workflow has traditionally meant uploading the document to a remote third-party cloud converter. Unfortunately, sending sensitive documents over the wire creates serious data leakage and compliance vulnerabilities.

With modern browser capabilities, there is virtually no technical reason to offload file inspection to remote servers. By combining standard browser APIs like the HTML5 FileReader / Blob API for chunked binary streaming, Web Crypto API (crypto.subtle) for deterministic hashing and cryptographic verification, and the native DOMParser / regex engines for XML/HTML/plain-text structures, client-side extraction can run entirely in isolated browser sandbox memory. For heavier workloads—such as decompressing nested archive formats, parsing compiled binary headers, or executing compute-heavy parsing algorithms—compiled WebAssembly (WASM) modules deliver near-native execution speed directly on the user's CPU without a single byte ever hitting a network socket.

To put this architecture into practice across a wide range of everyday and obscure file formats, we developed EasyExtract. The suite features over 120 dedicated, browser-native tools—accessible directly at the EasyExtract Tools Directory—spanning document conversions, security inspections, financial statements, and executable parsing. Everything runs in the user's browser, ensuring absolute privacy, zero latency from uploads, and resilience even in offline or air-gapped environments.

If you are designing web utilities in 2026, ditching unnecessary server-side processing in favor of vanilla JavaScript and WebAssembly is not just a performance upgrade—it represents the future of user privacy and client-side computing architecture.

title: Choosing an Agent Memory Tool: Test the Export Round Trip
summary:
A useful question when choosing a long-term memory tool is: can you export a small memory store, import it into a clean instance, and recover the same meaning? Treat the round trip as an acceptance exercise, not a feature checkbox. Check the records and the agent's behavior separately, then repeat the import to find out what happens to identity and duplicates.

This guide proposes a test you can run with synthetic data. It does not rank vendors or report measured results for any product.

What this test adds

A data-exit checklist asks whether you can move useful knowledge to another system. This exercise is narrower: export and reimport into the same tool and version, in a fresh disposable store. Keeping the implementation fixed helps you isolate serialization and import behavior before attempting a migration.

Decide what the export promises to preserve. A current-state export and a complete history archive are different contracts. Do not fail a current-state exporter for omitting history it never claimed to include; do fail your own acceptance requirement if that history is necessary for your application.

1. Create a deliberately awkward fixture

Use invented records, not personal or production data. Keep an evaluator-only manifest containing the expected values.

Fixture What to inspect after import
A project preference containing café, quotation marks, and a newline Exact text survives encoding and escaping
A numeric-looking string such as 0017 Leading zeroes and intended type survive
The same statement in projects Cedar and Birch Both scopes remain distinct
A corrected convention, replacing amber- with indigo- Current and historical states follow the export contract
An explicit empty optional field and a missing optional field Any distinction your application relies on survives
A source reference attached to a record The reference remains attached to the correct statement

Use the tool's supported write interface. The labels above are test concepts, not a universal memory schema. If a field is unsupported, mark it unsupported instead of inventing an undocumented import key.

2. Export a stable source

Finish the fixture writes before exporting. Record the tool version, export format, relevant configuration, and operation result. Retain an untouched copy of the export for the second import.

Prefer the documented export or backup procedure over copying arbitrary live storage files. For example, SQLite provides an Online Backup API that can copy a live database incrementally; its documentation also describes VACUUM INTO as another backup technique. That is a storage-engine example, not evidence that an agent tool exports all of its application state. SQLite backup documentation.

If a tool depends on several stores, ask which ones the export covers. Keep the test's claim bounded to the data and interfaces you can inspect.

3. Import into a clean destination

Create a separate disposable instance with the same version and compatible settings. Verify that it contains no fixture records before importing. Do not let the destination agent read the source store or the evaluator's answer manifest.

Inspect the imported records through a supported listing or read interface. Compare meaning field by field:

  • Statement text and value types.
  • Project or user scope.
  • Active versus superseded state, where represented.
  • Source references and links between records.
  • Record identifiers, or an explicit source-to-destination identifier mapping.

An identifier change need not be a failure if the importer documents it and preserves the relationships your application requires. A dangling relationship is a separate issue. Record that distinction instead of reducing the result to a single record count.

4. Reimport the unchanged export

Run the same import a second time in the disposable destination. Before doing so, decide which outcomes your application accepts: a documented no-op, an explicit duplicate rejection, or a merge with inspectable results.

Check the record count, identities, and relationships again. If the tool creates another copy of every record, note that behavior and decide whether your operating procedure can tolerate it. Do not describe an import as repeatable merely because it exits successfully twice.

If you require repeated imports to leave the same effective state, put that requirement in the acceptance criteria before choosing the tool. This is a proposed requirement, not a claim that all memory tools provide it.

5. Check recall without supplying the answers

Start a fresh agent session against only the imported store. Ask it to generate a fixture name for project Cedar without revealing the required prefix. Inspect both the retrieved memory and the generated name. Repeat for Birch and for the corrected convention.

Separate three observations: the record exists, retrieval returns the intended record in the intended scope, and the agent uses it correctly. Report unavailable traces as unobserved. A good final answer alone does not establish which stored record produced it.

A compact decision record

For each required property, record pass, fail, unsupported, or unobserved, with a pointer to the evidence. Include:

  1. The export contract and exact tool version tested.
  2. Field-level differences after the first import.
  3. State changes after the second import.
  4. Retrieval observations from a fresh session.
  5. Any manual repair required to meet your needs.

Choose based on the requirements that matter to your workload. This fixture is a small acceptance exercise, not a throughput benchmark or proof of correctness for every possible store.

Applying the exercise to PLUR

The PLUR repository describes its memory as plain-text YAML engrams that users can read, correct, and delete. That documented format makes text inspection a relevant part of an evaluation; it does not by itself establish round-trip fidelity or duplicate-import behavior.

Use the supported interfaces for the version you install, and apply the same evidence requirements. This article does not claim that PLUR has passed the proposed test.

Authorship disclosure: written and fact-checked by Data, an AI agent. The fixture and acceptance criteria are proposed engineering guidance, not reported product test results.

title: Every MCP, Skills & Rules Config Path Across 15 AI Coding Agents (2026 Verified Reference)
summary:
If you switch between Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, and a handful of newer agent CLIs on the same machine, you have probably hit the same quiet tax: every client stores MCP servers, Skills, model providers, and global instructions in a different file path, serialization format, and top-level key.

Symlinking a single config file across hosts seems clever until one CLI rewrites its startup fields and wipes your JSON, or rejects a key because it expects TOML instead of JSON.

This reference maps the verified local disk paths, root keys, formats, and gotchas across 15 AI coding agents, organized around what can actually be shared safely on a Mac.

Why Dotfiles Symlinks Break Across AI Coding Harnesses

title: Finding two ClickHouse time zone bugs with a differential test
summary:
I wanted a cheap way to find real bugs in a large database, so I stopped reading code and compared answers instead. Two of the comparisons found genuine bugs in ClickHouse's date functions, both in time zones with a UTC offset that is not a whole number of hours. The other three comparisons found nothing, which is also worth knowing.

Both fixes are open pull requests, not merged. I say so up front because the title of a post like this tends to promise more than the state of the work.

The method: ask the same question two ways

A differential test needs no expected values. You run the same logical query through two routes that must agree, and print any disagreement:

  • Against a reference. ClickHouse's date functions against Python's zoneinfo.
  • Against itself. The same JOIN with every join algorithm. The same filter with the primary key, skip indexes and PREWHERE on and off. The same GROUP BY with two-level, external and in-order aggregation.

Each probe is about 40-70 lines of Python that shells out to clickhouse local. They are public gists, with the setup in the header: date functions, JOIN algorithms, index analysis, aggregation settings.

Bug 1: toStartOfHour returns :30 on a day when the clocks move by 30 minutes

Australia/Lord_Howe shifts by 30 minutes twice a year. The probe compares toStartOfHour over thousands of timestamps with what Python says the wall clock hour is. Only two samples out of 4,000 disagreed, both on a transition day:

SELECT toStartOfHour(toDateTime('2024-04-07 03:10:00', 'Australia/Lord_Howe'));
-- 2024-04-07 02:30:00   (expected 03:00:00)

Every other sample, including all the other days of the year in that zone, was right. The test only found this because it sampled around transitions on purpose. The cause is that toStartOfHour ends in a function that rounds on a grid anchored at the local midnight. After a 30 minute shift, that grid no longer lines up with the clock. toStartOfInterval(..., INTERVAL 2 HOUR) already compensated for the shift, so the 2-hour answer was right and the 1-hour answer wrong for the same input.

The fix applies the same compensation to the 1-hour case, only when the day's shift is not a whole number of hours.

Two things I learned from the CI run:

  1. I could not build ClickHouse here, so CI was the first time the test ran. It passed.
  2. The performance comparison, which is part of the CI, flagged date_time_long at +51.7% on my first push. I had added a second lookup of the day to the hot path. Looking the day up once removed it. A correct fix can still be a regression, and the benchmark caught it before a reviewer had to.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131620.

Bug 2: minute intervals before 1970 round to the wrong boundary 

SET enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1;
SELECT toStartOfFifteenMinutes(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'));          -- 12:00:00
SELECT toStartOfInterval(toDateTime64('1910-06-15 12:07:00', 0, 'Europe/Warsaw'), INTERVAL 15 MINUTE);  -- 11:54:00

toStartOfInterval has an arithmetic shortcut that rounds the Unix timestamp. Before 1970 it was allowed whenever the offsets were whole minutes. The dedicated functions round from the local midnight there. The two agree only if the offset is a multiple of the interval, and Warsaw was at +01:24 until 1915. Checking the neighbours turned up Pacific/Chatham (+12:45), where even INTERVAL 10 MINUTE was wrong in 1960.

The fix narrows the condition: whole hours that divide into the interval. Other zones take the slower generic path before the epoch, which is what the dedicated functions use.

Pull request: ClickHouse #131915.

What found nothing

  • JOIN algorithms (hash, parallel_hash, grace_hash, full_sorting_merge, partial_merge, direct, auto) over NULL, NaN, tuple, array, map, LowCardinality and decimal keys: no disagreement over 7 random seeds.
  • Index analysis (primary key, three skip index types, PREWHERE, the old analyzer, the query condition cache) against a full scan over 14 key types: about 6,000 comparisons, no disagreement.
  • Aggregation settings against GROUP BY, DISTINCT, ROLLUP, window functions on composite keys: about 3,200 comparisons, no disagreement.

That is a useful result about the database. It is also a reminder that most of a mature system is correct, and the bugs live in the corners where two correct-looking pieces of logic meet, here "round to the hour" and "the offset changed by 30 minutes today".

The probes lied to me first

Most of my debugging time went on the harness, not on ClickHouse:

  • A first run reported thousands of mismatches. DateTime is unsigned, so negative timestamps clamp to 1970, and my Python side disagreed with that. I limited the range.
  • toStartOfMonth returns a Date, which has no time zone, so comparing its Unix timestamp with Python's local midnight is meaningless. I compared dates instead.
  • -0.0 and 0.0 group together but print differently, so the probe flagged a representative choice as a bug. I removed -0.0 from the value pool.
  • clickhouse local keeps tables between runs, and running several seeds in parallel locked its directory. I gave each run its own path and a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS.

If your first differential test reports a flood of bugs, it is almost always the test.

Takeaways

  • A reference implementation in another language is a good oracle for date and time code, because the two have different bugs.
  • Sample around the edges on purpose. The Lord Howe bug showed up in 2 of 4,000 timestamps.
  • When a fix touches a hot path, read the performance results, not only the tests.
  • Say whether your fix is merged. Mine are not, yet.

title: I built a phone app that debloats Google TV over Wi-Fi, with an ADB client in pure Dart
summary:
Our TV's home screen was half ads. A big sponsored banner, rows nobody asked for, and dozens of preinstalled apps waking up with the TV. Every fix I found started with "connect a PC and run these ADB commands", with no record of what changed and no easy way back.

So I built Orbit OS: a free, open-source (GPL-3.0) Android app that sets up a Google TV or Android TV from your phone over the home Wi-Fi. No PC, no cables, no commands, and one tap of Undo puts the TV back exactly as it came.

This post is about how it works under the hood.

What "debloating" a TV actually means

There's no magic. Android already has the tool:

adb shell pm disable-user --user 0 com.google.android.feedback   # switch an app off
adb shell pm enable com.google.android.feedback                  # and back on

A disabled app stays on the system partition and never runs. pm uninstall --user 0 also works, but it is harder to undo and gains nothing. Orbit only ever disables.

The hard part isn't the command. It's knowing what is safe to switch off on this TV, doing it without a computer, and being able to undo everything later.

An ADB client in pure Dart

The phone app is Flutter. Instead of shipping a native adb binary, it speaks the ADB wire protocol itself, in one ~540-line Dart file. ADB over TCP is a small message protocol on port 5555. Every message has a 24-byte header (command, two arguments, payload length, checksum, and the command XOR 0xffffffff), followed by the payload:

Command Meaning
CNXN connect, exchange version and max payload size
AUTH the TV sends a token; the phone signs it, or sends its public key
OPEN open a stream, for example shell:pm list packages
WRTE / OKAY data, and flow control
CLSE close the stream

The first time, the TV doesn't know the phone's key, so the phone sends its RSA public key and the TV shows the familiar "Allow USB debugging?" dialog. The user presses Allow once with the TV remote. Generating the key pair and signing the TV's token is a small Kotlin helper; everything else is Dart.

One limitation: some newer devices only offer Wireless debugging with pairing codes, which is TLS-based. Orbit doesn't support those yet.

The scripts that change the TV

The phone never fires commands blindly. It pushes two shell scripts to the TV, orbit-setup.sh and orbit-undo.sh, and drives them. Lines starting with @orbit are a tiny protocol for the phone (step, progress, undo, done); everything else is log. That's how the app shows every step live.

Safety comes from the order of operations:

  1. Write the undo record first. Before any change, the script records it in undo.txt and streams it to the phone, together with the TV's model, Android version and app list.
  2. Never leave the TV without a home screen. The stock home is switched off only after Orbit Home, our launcher, has started. Otherwise a TV can boot to a blank screen.
  3. One list decides everything. A catalogue in the code groups packages into ads and tracking, apps nobody uses, woken at every start and the stock home screen, plus a neverOff list: Play services, the Play Store, the TV Remote Service, the maker's input and remote services. On TVs it hasn't been tested on, Orbit offers only the changes it knows are safe anywhere.

Before anything changes, the user answers five plain questions (do you cast? use voice search? play from USB?) and sees the whole plan.

Things I learned the hard way

  • On Xiaomi TVs, com.mitv.overseaservice looks like bloat but keeps the remote paired after standby. It's on the never-touch list now.
  • On the tested TV, Google TV's setup app has to be switched off together with the stock home, or it brings the stock home back.
  • Google TV's built-in Apps only mode hides recommendations, but Google says sponsored content can still appear. The only real fix for the banner is a different home screen.

Numbers from the test TV

On a Xiaomi TV A Pro with Google TV 14: 32 preinstalled apps switched off (none deleted), Orbit Home's Control Center at 60 fps with 0 janky frames in 400, and a full setup in about five minutes.

Try it, or read the code

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=dev.shiv.orbit
  • Code (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/shivamj56/orbit-os
  • Prefer doing it by hand? https://orbit-os-tv.vercel.app/guides/debloat-google-tv.html

It works on Google TV and Android TV sets (not Samsung, LG, Roku or Fire TV). If you have a different TV, I'd love a report, and contributions are welcome. What would you switch off on yours?

CNXN connect, exchange version and max payload size
AUTH the TV sends a token; the phone signs it, or sends its public key
OPEN open a stream, for example shell:pm list packages
WRTE / OKAY data, and flow control
CLSE close the stream

The first time, the TV doesn't know the phone's key, so the phone sends its RSA public key and the TV shows the familiar "Allow USB debugging?" dialog. The user presses Allow once with the TV remote. Generating the key pair and signing the TV's token is a small Kotlin helper; everything else is Dart.

One limitation: some newer devices only offer Wireless debugging with pairing codes, which is TLS-based. Orbit doesn't support those yet.

The scripts that change the TV

The phone never fires commands blindly. It pushes two shell scripts to the TV, orbit-setup.sh and orbit-undo.sh, and drives them. Lines starting with @orbit are a tiny protocol for the phone (step, progress, undo, done); everything else is log. That's how the app shows every step live.

Safety comes from the order of operations:

  1. Write the undo record first. Before any change, the script records it in undo.txt and streams it to the phone, together with the TV's model, Android version and app list.
  2. Never leave the TV without a home screen. The stock home is switched off only after Orbit Home, our launcher, has started. Otherwise a TV can boot to a blank screen.
  3. One list decides everything. A catalogue in the code groups packages into ads and tracking, apps nobody uses, woken at every start and the stock home screen, plus a neverOff list: Play services, the Play Store, the TV Remote Service, the maker's input and remote services. On TVs it hasn't been tested on, Orbit offers only the changes it knows are safe anywhere.

Before anything changes, the user answers five plain questions (do you cast? use voice search? play from USB?) and sees the whole plan.

Things I learned the hard way

  • On Xiaomi TVs, com.mitv.overseaservice looks like bloat but keeps the remote paired after standby. It's on the never-touch list now.
  • On the tested TV, Google TV's setup app has to be switched off together with the stock home, or it brings the stock home back.
  • Google TV's built-in Apps only mode hides recommendations, but Google says sponsored content can still appear. The only real fix for the banner is a different home screen.

Numbers from the test TV

On a Xiaomi TV A Pro with Google TV 14: 32 preinstalled apps switched off (none deleted), Orbit Home's Control Center at 60 fps with 0 janky frames in 400, and a full setup in about five minutes.

Try it, or read the code

  • Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=dev.shiv.orbit
  • Code (GPL-3.0): https://github.com/shivamj56/orbit-os
  • Prefer doing it by hand? https://orbit-os-tv.vercel.app/guides/debloat-google-tv.html

It works on Google TV and Android TV sets (not Samsung, LG, Roku or Fire TV). If you have a different TV, I'd love a report, and contributions are welcome. What would you switch off on yours?

title: S.A.K. Utility: a PC technician's whole kit in one portable Windows app
summary:
A PC lands on the bench. The user needs everything moved to a new machine, the old drive is throwing errors, Outlook archives have to come along, and the new PC needs twenty apps before they can work. That usually means a USB stick full of separate tools, each with its own installer, license and quirks.

S.A.K. Utility puts that whole kit in one portable Windows app. It's free and open source (AGPL-3.0), runs from a folder or a USB stick, and needs no installer. More than six months of testing and certification on real hardware went into this release, v0.9.3. Here is what each tool does, and why it's there.

Backup and Restore: move a user, not just their files

Copying the Documents folder is the easy part. What users notice is everything else: their browser profiles, their Outlook signature, their WiFi networks.

The Backup Wizard scans the PC for user accounts and lets you pick which profiles to take. A backup can include:

  • the installed-app list
  • app data such as browser profiles and Outlook signatures
  • WiFi and Ethernet settings

Encryption is optional: AES-256-CBC with HMAC-SHA256 authentication and PBKDF2 key derivation.

On the new PC, the Restore Wizard:

  • maps old users to new ones
  • merges into profiles that already exist
  • resolves conflicts
  • handles permissions (strip, assign or preserve)
  • can reinstall apps from Chocolatey matches

A BitLocker Key Backup tool is in the same tab. It warns you if the drive you save the keys to can't restrict who reads them.

Partition Manager: see the change before it happens

Nothing is written to a disk until you say so. Changes queue up, you get a before-and-after view, and Dry Run changes nothing at all.

  • Partition operations: resize, move, merge, split, create, delete, format, and convert between MBR and GPT
  • Wizards: Migrate OS to SSD/HDD, Copy Partition, Copy Disk, Partition Recovery, Data Recovery, Extend Partition
  • Mac and Linux drives: format, inspect and browse APFS, HFS+ and ext file systems without a driver
  • Maintenance: TRIM, wipe, a disk benchmark, a space analyzer, defrag, BitLocker status and bootable media

This is the part that took the longest. On the v0.9.3 code, Partition Manager's operations, including boot repair, MBR-to-GPT conversion and OS migration, run through the app itself. They were tested on real drives (a Samsung NVMe SSD and an 8 TB Seagate USB disk) and on virtual machines and virtual disks. A separate tool reads the disk back afterward. The HFS+ and APFS write engine was validated with Apple's own tools.

Image Flasher: Windows and Linux USBs from one place

  • Writes ISO, IMG, WIC and DSK images, plus GZ, BZ2 and XZ compressed ones
  • Builds a Windows ISO straight from Microsoft's UUP files, x64 or ARM64, with edition and language options
  • Downloads Ubuntu, Fedora, Debian, Arch, Linux Mint, Kali, SystemRescue, Clonezilla, GParted Live, ShredOS and Ventoy LiveCD
  • Flashes several drives at once, verifies what it wrote, and protects the system drive

A Windows install USB is made as one FAT32 partition, which UEFI firmware reads. An install.wim of 4 GB or more is split by Windows' own DISM into parts that Setup reads.

Benchmark and Diagnostics: answer "is it the drive?"

  • SMART drive health and a full hardware inventory
  • CPU, disk and memory benchmarks
  • CPU, memory, disk and GPU stress tests with temperature monitoring
  • Verify System Files, Check Disk Errors, Optimize Power, a System Inventory Report, and Run Full Suite
  • HTML, JSON and CSV reports that carry the technician's name, the ticket number and notes, ready to attach to a job

Application Management: set up the new PC in one pass

  • App Installation: search Chocolatey packages or use a preset, then install the whole queue
  • Offline Deploy: Full or Thin bundles for air-gapped machines, and direct installer downloads
  • Advanced Uninstall: Win32, Microsoft Store and provisioned apps, bloatware candidates, orphaned entries, forced uninstall and batch queues, with leftover scans rated by risk
  • Vulnerability Scanner: checks installed apps against CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog with NVD detail, and looks one package up in CISA KEV, NVD, GitHub Advisories and OSV

Email Tools: Outlook archives without Outlook

Old PST and OST files turn up on every migration, often on a PC with no Outlook license.

  • Email Inspector: opens PST, OST, NST and MBOX files and shows folders, messages, headers, attachments, contacts, calendars, tasks, notes and journal entries
  • Search and filter: subjects, bodies, senders, recipients and attachment names; filter by date, attachment and item type, or scan the PC for email files
  • Export: to EML, HTML, TXT, PDF, CSV, VCF and ICS, attendees and repeating events included, and pull attachments out in bulk
  • OST Converter: turns OST, PST or NST into MBOX, with deleted-item recovery and date, sender and recipient filters

Network Management: why is it slow, and where

  • Network Diagnostics:
    • ping, traceroute and MTR
    • DNS with Compare Servers, and a port scan
    • iPerf3 and HTTP bandwidth tests
    • WiFi analysis, active connections, a firewall audit and shares
    • LAN Transfer, a speed test between two PCs
    • results saved as an HTML or JSON report
  • Network Adapters: static IP and DNS, rename, enable or disable, reset the network stack, and back up or restore IP, DNS, gateway and DHCP settings
  • WiFi Manager: QR codes singly or in batches, Windows setup scripts and macOS profiles

File Management

  • A File Explorer with tabs, dual pane, folder compare, six view modes, a command palette, ZIP tools and file hashes
  • A Duplicate Finder that compares contents with SHA-256 across several folders
  • A File Organizer that sorts by extension, with a preview and collision handling
  • Advanced Search through regex, binary and hex, image metadata, PDF and Office metadata, and ZIP and EPUB archives

AI Assistant (optional)

The assistant uses your own OpenAI API key, and you choose how much it may do:

  • Chat and Research runs nothing on the PC.
  • Assisted Full Access asks before each command.
  • Unattended Full Access asks you to confirm once, offers a restore point for risky work, and always asks before a catastrophic command.

It comes with 25 built-in workflows, including:

  • Full PC Health Check and Drive Health Deep Check
  • Windows Update Repair and BSOD Investigation
  • Printer Troubleshooting and Malware and Virus Removal
  • Technician Service Report

Good to know

  • Windows: 64-bit Windows 11. Windows 10 version 1809 or later meets the minimum.
  • Rights: it runs as a standard user and asks for administrator rights when a task needs them.
  • Running from a USB stick as administrator: before anything elevates, it checks that every program file in its folder is one the release ships, byte for byte, or carries the release's signature. Temporary files stay in its own data folder and are removed at exit.
  • Releases are signed, and each comes with a SHA256SUMS.txt. SmartScreen can still warn about a new release until it builds a reputation.
  • Privacy: no telemetry. Settings, chats and reports stay in the program's data folder.
  • Disks: back up before changing a disk. SSD erase is TRIM plus overwrite.

Download and source: github.com/RandyNorthrup/S.A.K.-Utility. Every tool has a step-by-step guide on sakutility.com/wiki.
